You are reconstructing the precise semantics of the mapbox "earcut" polygon triangulation algorithm (the C++ header-only port, earcut.hpp, whose API is mapbox::earcut<N>(polygon) -> std::vector<N> of triangle vertex indices into the flattened concatenation of all rings; ring 0 is the outer ring, rings 1..k are holes).

The library source is NOT available on disk and you must NOT try to download it. Reconstruct from your knowledge of this well-known public algorithm. Do not search the local filesystem for it (it is absent). Do not use WebFetch/WebSearch.

CRITICAL: the goal is a byte-for-byte identical reimplementation, so the EXACT ORDER in which triangles are emitted matters, as do exact comparison operators (>= vs >), exact traversal directions, exact tie-breaks, and exact floating-point expression forms (do not algebraically rearrange - "(q.y-p.y)*(r.x-q.x) - (q.x-p.x)*(r.y-q.y)" must stay in that form).

Report pseudocode at the level of literal translatable statements.

YOUR SUBSYSTEM: the z-order (Morton code) spatial hash used for large polygons.

Reconstruct exactly:
1. zOrder(x, y): the transform "int32_t x = (x_ - minX) * inv_size" (a C-style truncating cast toward zero), then the bit-interleave shifts/masks (0x00FF00FF, 0x0F0F0F0F, 0x33333333, 0x55555555) and the final "x | (y << 1)". State whether earcut.hpp uses inv_size (multiply) or size (divide), and the 32767 constant.
2. indexCurve(start): "p->z = p->z ? p->z : zOrder(p->x, p->y)", setting prevZ/nextZ from prev/next, then breaking the circle (p->prevZ->nextZ = null; p->prevZ = null) and calling sortLinked.
3. sortLinked(list): the exact bottom-up merge sort on the nextZ/prevZ chain (inSize doubling, pSize/qSize, the "p->z <= q->z" comparison for stability, tail wiring, numMerges <= 1 termination). This ordering is observable in output, so be precise.
4. isEarHashed(ear): the triangle bbox, minZ/maxZ from zOrder of the bbox corners, the simultaneous prevZ/nextZ walk "while (p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ)", the per-candidate guards (bbox containment check present in newer versions; "p != ear->prev && p != ear->next"), then the two tail loops. Describe version differences in whether the bbox containment pre-check exists inside the loops.
5. Exactly when hashing is enabled and when indexCurve is called (only when pass == 0).

content.text: I'll reconstruct this from knowledge of the mapbox earcut.hpp source (v2.2.x master) and its JS counterpart (earcut 2.2.4), which the C++ port tracks line-for-line.

input.determinismNotes:
GENERAL

- All z values are `int32_t` (member `Node::z`, default-initialized to `0`). All coordinates are `double`. `inv_size`, `minX`, `minY`, `maxX`, `maxY` are `double` members of the `Earcut<N>` functor; `hashing` is a `bool` member.
- earcut.hpp uses the RECIPROCAL form: `inv_size = 32767. / (max span)`, and zOrder MULTIPLIES by it. It does NOT divide by a `size`. (Old earcut 2.0.x JS used `x = 32767 * (x - minX) / size;` — the C++ port and modern JS both use the multiply-by-invSize form. Using the divide form gives bit-different results for some inputs because `(a-b)*(32767/s)` != `32767*(a-b)/s` in IEEE754, and the truncating cast can then land on a different integer, changing z, changing sort order, changing emitted triangle order. This must be reproduced exactly.)
- The cast is a C-style/`static_cast<int32_t>` truncation toward zero, equivalent to JS `| 0`. Inputs are always >= 0 because minX/minY come from a full scan of the same node set, so truncation == floor here, but write it as a truncating cast anyway.
- Degenerate case: if `maxX-minX` and `maxY-minY` are both 0, `inv_size` is set to `.0` (not inf). Then every z is 0 and the sort is a stable no-op. `hashing` is still true.
- Bit-interleave arithmetic never overflows: inputs are in [0, 32767] (15 bits), spread to bits 0,2,...,28; `y << 1` occupies bits 1,3,...,29. Result fits in int32 positive range. No UB from the `<< 8` etc. since values stay under 2^30.

ORDERING / OBSERVABILITY

- `sortLinked` is a bottom-up (Simon Tatham) merge sort and is STABLE via `p->z <= q->z` (take from the left/`p` run on ties). Using `<` instead would swap equal-z nodes and change which candidate `isEarHashed` encounters first — but more importantly it changes nothing about correctness while changing nothing observable *unless* the walk terminates early; still, reproduce `<=` exactly.
- Ties in z are extremely common (all duplicate coordinates, and any two points that quantize into the same 15x15-bit cell), so stability is load-bearing for byte-identical output in practice.
- The initial order fed to `sortLinked` is the ring order starting at `start` (the node `indexCurve` was called with), broken between `start->prev` and `start`. So the pre-sort sequence is start, start->next, ..., start->prev. Changing which node `earcutLinked` was entered at changes the pre-sort permutation and therefore the post-sort order of equal-z nodes.
- `indexCurve` DISCARDS the head returned by `sortLinked`. Nothing ever traverses from the head; all traversal starts at `ear->prevZ` / `ear->nextZ`. Do not "fix" this.
- `isEarHashed` short-circuits on the FIRST blocking candidate found. The order of the two halves of the simultaneous loop body (p-side checked and advanced first, then n-side) is observable only via performance, not result — but the loop's *termination condition* (`p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ`, all four ANDed) is observable, because it decides which of the two tail loops runs and how far.
- `area(...) >= 0` (not `>`) both as the reflex test and as the candidate-is-reflex test. `pointInTriangle` uses three `>= 0` tests. Do not change any to `>`.
- Keep the cross-product expression forms verbatim: `area(p,q,r) = (q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`.

Z-CHAIN MAINTENANCE

- `removeNode(p)` also unlinks p from the z chain (`if (p->prevZ) p->prevZ->nextZ = p->nextZ; if (p->nextZ) p->nextZ->prevZ = p->prevZ;`). Every node removal (ear cut, `filterPoints`, `cureLocalIntersections`) therefore keeps the z chain consistent. Nodes newly created by `splitPolygon` are NOT inserted into the z chain; they get `z == 0`, `prevZ == nextZ == nullptr`, and are only integrated when a later `indexCurve` runs over their ring (i.e. via `splitEarcut` -> `earcutLinked(a)` with pass 0).
- Because `splitEarcut` calls `earcutLinked(a)` / `earcutLinked(c)` with the default `pass = 0`, `indexCurve` runs AGAIN on each half when hashing is on. `p->z = p->z ? p->z : zOrder(p->x, p->y)` means already-computed z values are reused verbatim and only new/zero-z nodes are computed. A node whose true zOrder is exactly 0 (a point at the bbox min corner) is harmlessly recomputed every time. Reproduce the ternary, not an `if (p->z == 0)`.

functions.name: operator() — hashing enablement and bbox / inv_size setup
functions.signature: template <typename Polygon> void Earcut<N>::operator()(const Polygon& points)
functions.notes: HASHING IS ENABLED IFF the total number of input vertices summed over rings exceeds 80 (threshold starts at 80, each ring's size is subtracted while threshold >= 0; hashing = threshold < 0). Exactly 80 total vertices => threshold == 0 => hashing == FALSE. 81 => hashing == TRUE. The bbox scan happens AFTER eliminateHoles, so it walks the single merged ring and therefore covers every hole vertex too (holes were bridged in with duplicated nodes). minX/minY/inv_size are computed once and never recomputed, even after splitEarcut. `inv_size` defaults to 0 as a member; when hashing is false it is never read. Note the doubled `inv_size` assignment: it temporarily holds the span, then is overwritten with the reciprocal — reproduce the `!= .0` guard so a zero-area bbox yields inv_size == 0.0 rather than inf/NaN.

functions.name: zOrder
functions.signature: int32_t Earcut<N>::zOrder(const double x_, const double y_)
functions.notes: MULTIPLY BY inv_size — earcut.hpp stores the reciprocal `inv_size = 32767. / max(maxX-minX, maxY-minY)` and multiplies here. It does NOT store a `size` and divide. The 32767 constant lives in the setup code (operator()), NOT in zOrder; zOrder itself contains no 32767. The cast is a truncation toward zero (equivalent to JS `x = (x - minX) * invSize | 0`). Both axes use the SAME inv_size (isotropic scaling off the larger span), so the shorter axis does not use its full 15 bits. Shift/mask sequence order is 8/0x00FF00FF, 4/0x0F0F0F0F, 2/0x33333333, 1/0x55555555 for each axis independently; x occupies even bits, y is shifted left one into odd bits. Final combine is `x | (y << 1)` — x is the LOW bit of each pair. Intermediate `x << 8` on a 15-bit value cannot overflow int32.

functions.name: indexCurve
functions.notes: The z chain is seeded as an exact copy of the ring order (prevZ=prev, nextZ=next) traversed FORWARD from `start`, then the circle is cut between start->prev and start, making a linear list whose head is `start` and whose tail is `start->prev`. The pre-sort sequence is therefore start, start->next, ..., start->prev — this permutation determines the relative order of equal-z nodes after the stable sort, so the identity of `start` is observable in the final triangle order. `p->z ? p->z : zOrder(...)` reuses any previously computed z (matters on the second and later indexCurve calls triggered by splitEarcut, and for nodes created by splitPolygon which arrive with z == 0). The `sortLinked` return value is dropped; the sorted list is only ever reached through per-node prevZ/nextZ pointers.

functions.name: sortLinked
functions.notes: Bottom-up merge sort over the nextZ/prevZ chain, in place, no allocation. Key exactness points: (1) the pSize counting loop runs `inSize` times but breaks early when q hits null — pSize ends as the ACTUAL length of the left run; (2) qSize is optimistically set to inSize and is bounds-checked by the `!q` / `qSize > 0 && q` conditions; (3) the branch cascade order is exactly: pSize==0 -> take q; qSize==0 || !q -> take p; p->z <= q->z -> take p; else take q. The `<=` makes the sort STABLE (equal z keeps original relative order) and is directly observable in output for polygons with duplicate/co-cell points; (4) prevZ is rewired on every emitted element (`e->prevZ = tail`) so the result is a correct doubly-linked list; (5) `tail->nextZ = nullptr` after each pass is an UNGUARDED dereference — safe only because sortLinked is never called with an empty list (indexCurve always passes a non-null ring); (6) termination is `numMerges <= 1` checked AFTER the tail fixup and BEFORE doubling inSize, so the final pass's list is returned; (7) `inSize *= 2` at the bottom of the outer loop. The returned head is discarded by the only caller.

functions.name: isEarHashed
functions.notes:
STRUCTURE: one simultaneous bidirectional loop whose guard is the 4-way conjunction `p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ` (so it stops as soon as EITHER direction is exhausted), followed by two single-direction tail loops that drain whichever side still has range left. The p-side always uses `>= minZ` and walks prevZ; the n-side always uses `<= maxZ` and walks nextZ. Both bounds are INCLUSIVE.

GUARDS: the bbox-containment pre-check (`p->x >= minTX && p->x <= maxTX && p->y >= minTY && p->y <= maxTY`) is a pure fast-reject and is semantically redundant with pointInTriangle — it changes no results, only speed. VERSION DIFFERENCE: in the modern source (earcut 2.2.3+/2.2.4, matching earcut.hpp master) the bbox pre-check is present in ALL THREE loops. In the simultaneous loop it is written FIRST (before the identity checks) and the identity checks are written as `p !== a && p !== c`; in the two tail loops the identity checks come FIRST and are written as `p !== ear.prev && p !== ear.next`. `a == ear->prev` and `c == ear->next` so the two spellings are identical in effect. In OLDER versions (earcut <= 2.1.x, earcut.hpp <= ~0.12) there is NO simultaneous loop at all: it is two sequential loops, first `p = ear->nextZ; while (p && p->z <= maxZ)` then `p = ear->prevZ; while (p && p->z >= minZ)`, each with only `p != ear->prev && p != ear->next && pointInTriangle(...) && area(p->prev,p,p->next) >= 0` and NO bbox pre-check. The old and new forms return the same boolean, so triangle output is identical; only the traversal cost differs.

Note the ear node itself is never a false positive: `p`/`n` start one step away in the z chain, and `ear` cannot be its own prevZ/nextZ. But `ear` CAN be revisited? No — the z chain is linear (not circular), so each walk terminates at null.

pointInTriangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy,px,py) == ((cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0) && ((ax-px)*(by-py) - (bx-px)*(ay-py) >= 0) && ((bx-px)*(cy-py) - (cx-px)*(by-py) >= 0). Keep all three as >= 0 and in that operand order.

MIN/MAX NESTING: reproduce `std::min<double>(a->x, std::min<double>(b->x, c->x))` exactly (inner pair is b,c). With NaN-free inputs this matches Math.min(ax,bx,cx); with NaNs it does not, but earcut is undefined on NaN input anyway.

functions.name: earcutLinked — indexCurve trigger and hashed/unhashed dispatch

input.subsystem: z-order (Morton code) spatial hash: zOrder, indexCurve, sortLinked, isEarHashed, and the hashing enablement path in operator()/earcutLinked (mapbox earcut.hpp v2.2.x)

uncertainties.what: Whether the bbox-containment pre-check (`p->x >= minTX && p->x <= maxTX && ...`) exists inside the loops of isEarHashed, and whether isEarHashed uses the modern simultaneous bidirectional walk or the older two-sequential-loops form.
uncertainties.alternatives: Modern (earcut 2.2.3+ / earcut.hpp master, what I reported): simultaneous `while (p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ)` plus two tail loops, bbox pre-check present in all three. Older (earcut <= 2.1.x / earcut.hpp <= ~0.12): two sequential loops, first nextZ ascending with `p->z <= maxZ`, then prevZ descending with `p->z >= minZ`, NO bbox pre-check. Both forms compute the same boolean, so the emitted triangle sequence is IDENTICAL either way — this is a performance-only divergence. If byte-identity is the goal you can safely pick either.
uncertainties.confidence: High that the modern form is what current earcut.hpp master contains; certain that the choice does not affect output.

uncertainties.what: Exact spelling of the identity guards in the simultaneous loop: `p != a && p != c` vs `p != ear->prev && p != ear->next`, and whether the identity checks precede or follow the bbox checks.
uncertainties.alternatives: JS 2.2.4 writes bbox-then-`p !== a && p !== c` in the simultaneous loop and `p !== ear.prev && p !== ear.next`-then-bbox in the tail loops. earcut.hpp may spell both as `ear->prev`/`ear->next` throughout. Since a == ear->prev and c == ear->next and all conjuncts are side-effect-free, every ordering is observationally equivalent.
uncertainties.confidence: High that it is semantically irrelevant; medium on the literal source spelling.

uncertainties.what: Whether earcutLinked declares an unused `int iterations = 0; iterations++;` counter.
uncertainties.alternatives: Some revisions of earcut.hpp carried a loop counter that was incremented but never read (a leftover). Present or absent, it has zero effect on output. I omitted it.

uncertainties.what: Whether the C++ member is named `inv_size` (snake) or `invSize`, and whether zOrder's parameters are `const double x_, const double y_`.
uncertainties.alternatives: earcut.hpp uses snake_case `inv_size` (unusual for the file, but I am fairly confident) with the trailing-underscore parameter names `x_`/`y_` to avoid shadowing the local `x`/`y`. Naming only; no semantic impact.

uncertainties.what: The exact threshold constant and comparison for enabling hashing.
uncertainties.alternatives: I reported `int threshold = 80;` decremented by each ring's size while `threshold >= 0`, then `hashing = threshold < 0`. This means hashing turns on strictly above 80 total vertices. An alternative reading some ports use is a direct `len > 80` test; these differ only at exactly 80/81 boundary semantics for multi-ring input (the short-circuiting loop stops early, so with many rings the decrement form is what matters). I am confident in the decrement form and the value 80.

uncertainties.what: Whether `Node::z` is `int32_t` initialized to 0 (C++) versus `null` (JS), affecting the `p->z ? p->z : zOrder(...)` idiom.
uncertainties.alternatives: C++ uses `int32_t z = 0;` and the ternary; JS 2.2.4 uses `this.z = 0` with `if (p.z === 0) p.z = zOrder(...)`, and JS 2.1.x used `null` with `p.z === null`. All three behave the same except for the pathological point whose true z is 0 (the bbox min corner), which the C++/modern-JS form recomputes redundantly — same value, no output difference.

uncertainties.what: Whether sortLinked is declared to return Node* and whether indexCurve discards it.
uncertainties.alternatives: It returns Node* (the new head) and indexCurve calls it as a bare statement, discarding the result. Some compilers warn; the library does not mark it nodiscard. Behaviorally settled: nothing reads the head.
